title: Lamentations 3:19–33
context: The afflicted man still speaks. He asks that his affliction and misery be remembered (3:19–20), then recalls what gives him hope (3:21): the LORD’s loving kindnesses, mercies that do not fail and are new every morning, and the LORD’s great faithfulness (3:22–23). The turn does not erase the lament before and after it; it rises from inside it, and the poem soon returns to grief. The “we” of 3:22 briefly draws the community into the man’s hope. In 3:25–30 he speaks in the manner of wisdom teaching about the good of waiting quietly, bearing the yoke, keeping silence, and humility, even giving the cheek to the one who strikes (compare Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 5:39). The section ends with three “for” clauses (3:31–33): the Lord will not cast off forever, his compassion follows the grief he causes, and he does not afflict willingly. Both traditions treat 3:22–33 as shared ground on mercy within judgment: the LORD truly brings affliction for sin, yet his loving kindness and faithfulness run deeper than his anger (compare Exodus 34:6–7; Psalm 30:5). Both also counsel care in using these lines with sufferers: they are hope voiced from within grief, not a slogan to silence it. The traditions explain “he does not afflict willingly” (3:33) within their own frameworks, but the pastoral point is held in common.

verses.text: Remember my affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the bitterness.
verses.arminianNotes: “Remember my affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the bitterness.” Arminian readers hear the man asking to be remembered, much as Zion has asked the LORD to look and see (1:9, 1:11, 2:20), and they see the plea as an act of trust that God responds to his people’s cry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers understand the plea not as reminding God of something forgotten but as asking him to act in covenant faithfulness, and they note that the wormwood and bitterness of 3:15 are now brought before him. Shared ground: both traditions read the request as faith speaking within grief, the first step of the turn toward hope.

verses.text: My soul still remembers them, and is bowed down within me.
verses.arminianNotes: The man’s soul “still remembers them, and is bowed down within me.” Arminian readers note that the memory of suffering does not vanish when hope begins, and they encourage patience with those whose grief lingers, since the poem itself lets the memory remain alongside the hope that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the bowed soul as the humility God’s discipline produces (compare Psalm 42:5–6), the posture in which hope is received as a gift. Shared ground: both traditions recognize that remembering pain is part of healing rather than a lack of faith, and that the turn to hope comes from within the lament.

verses.text: This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.
verses.arminianNotes: “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.” Arminian readers see a deliberate act of remembering, a choice to call to mind what is true of God, which grace enables and which the sufferer can make while grief remains; they note that hope rests on what he remembers of the LORD, not on any change in his situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see hope arising not from circumstances but from the truths about God that follow, and they stress that even the ability to recall them is God’s gift. Shared ground: both traditions read 3:21 as the hinge of the poem, where hope is grounded in God’s character, and both see the recalling as real human action sustained by grace.

verses.text: It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
verses.arminianNotes: “It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.” Arminian readers see God’s steadfast covenant love toward his people as the reason judgment has not ended in destruction, and they hear the shift to “we” drawing the community into the man’s hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same loving kindnesses as God’s faithful, covenant-keeping love, which sets the limit of judgment and ensures that his people are not wholly destroyed. Shared ground: both traditions treat this line as the heart of mercy in judgment and read it within the ruin of Jerusalem, not as a denial of the suffering around it.

verses.text: They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” Arminian readers hear daily mercy given afresh and a faithfulness that invites daily trust; they also note that the confession is spoken among the ruins, so it is offered to the grieving gently, not as a quick answer to their pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear God’s unchanging covenant faithfulness renewing its mercies each day, rooted in his own character rather than in his people’s deserving. Shared ground: both traditions cherish the line, and both hold that it belongs inside the lament, where the night has been long and the morning’s mercy is awaited in hope.

verses.text: “The LORD is my portion,” says my soul. “Therefore I will hope in him.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD is my portion,” says the man’s soul, echoing the Levites’ inheritance and the psalms (compare Numbers 18:20; Psalm 16:5; 73:26). Arminian readers see a personal claim of faith, made when land, temple, and prosperity are gone, and a renewed resolve to hope in him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD himself as the inheritance that cannot be lost, even when every earthly portion is taken, and they read the resolve to hope as the fruit of grace. Shared ground: both traditions hear a believer finding in God what the ruined city can no longer give, and both treat that hope as real and costly.

verses.text: The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.
verses.arminianNotes: The man speaks in the manner of wisdom teaching: “The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.” Arminian readers stress the invitation in waiting and seeking, a responsive posture God welcomes (compare Isaiah 40:31; Jeremiah 29:13), open to all who turn to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the same invitation and add that waiting and seeking are themselves evidence of God’s prior work in the heart (compare Psalm 27:14; Philippians 2:13). Shared ground: both traditions affirm the LORD’s goodness to those who wait for him, and both commend patient seeking in hard seasons.

verses.text: It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.” Arminian readers commend patient trust as a fitting response to grace in suffering, and they note that quiet waiting is not passivity but an active, persevering hope that keeps looking to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see salvation here as wholly the LORD’s work, which his people wait for rather than achieve, and they hear in “quietly” a call to rest in his timing (compare Psalm 62:1; Isaiah 30:15). Shared ground: both traditions read “salvation” here first as deliverance from the present ruin, and both commend hopeful waiting.

verses.text: It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
verses.arminianNotes: “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.” Arminian readers hear practical wisdom: discipline learned early forms character and trust, and the yoke may be the hardship of judgment accepted humbly rather than resisted with bitterness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the yoke as God’s fatherly discipline that trains his children (compare Hebrews 12:7–11), with the good it brings coming from his purpose rather than from suffering itself. Shared ground: both traditions take the line as wisdom about suffering, not a claim that suffering is good in itself, and both apply it gently.

verses.text: Let him sit alone and keep silence, because he has laid it on him.
verses.arminianNotes: “Let him sit alone and keep silence, because he has laid it on him.” Arminian readers see the silence as humility before God in a season of discipline, not a ban on lament, since the whole poem shows that the afflicted may speak honestly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the yoke is laid on by the LORD, so the sufferer can accept it as from his hand and wait without bitterness (compare Psalm 39:9). Shared ground: both traditions read the call to silence alongside the poem’s many cries, and both caution against using this line to hurry others into silence.

verses.text: Let him put his mouth in the dust, if it is so that there may be hope.
verses.arminianNotes: “Let him put his mouth in the dust, if it is so that there may be hope.” Arminian readers hear deep humility and a tentative “if” that keeps hope honest rather than presumptuous, and they see repentance as the path on which God’s mercy is met.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see bowing low as the posture of one who has no claim on God and looks only to his mercy, and they note that the hedged “if” does not deny hope but rests it entirely on God. Shared ground: both traditions value the humble realism of the line and read it as hope that does not presume.

verses.text: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him. Let him be filled full of reproach.
verses.arminianNotes: “Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him.” Arminian readers connect this with the servant who gave his cheeks to those who struck him (Isaiah 50:6) and with Jesus’ teaching on the other cheek (Matthew 5:39), and they hear a call to non-retaliation rather than an endorsement of abuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the acceptance of reproach as entrusting oneself to God, who judges justly (compare 1 Peter 2:23), and many trace the line to Christ’s own suffering. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as patient endurance under judgment, and both caution against using it to keep the vulnerable under ongoing abuse.

verses.text: For the Lord will not cast off forever.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the Lord will not cast off forever.” Arminian readers see the limit of judgment in God’s merciful purpose for his people (compare Psalm 77:7; 103:9), and they hear an invitation to trust that rejection is not his final word for those who turn to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same limit grounded in God’s covenant faithfulness, which ensures that he will not finally abandon his people even when he disciplines them severely. Shared ground: both traditions hear this as the first of three reasons for hope, and both offer it to sufferers as a promise about God, not a timetable.

verses.text: For though he causes grief, yet he will have compassion according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.
verses.arminianNotes: “Though he causes grief, yet he will have compassion according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.” Arminian readers see grief and compassion held together, with compassion as the deeper movement of God’s heart, and they note that the grief is real judgment, not mere appearance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who both brings grief and shows compassion, his sovereign hand directing both toward the good of his people. Shared ground: both traditions confess that God causes grief in judgment and that his loving kindnesses, the same word as in 3:22, are greater still.

verses.text: For he does not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.
verses.arminianNotes: “For he does not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.” Arminian readers hear God’s heart here: affliction is not his delight but a response to sin (compare Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11), and they see in the line God’s genuine goodwill toward all people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers distinguish what God ordains from what he delights in: he truly sends affliction, yet takes no pleasure in it for its own sake, and uses it for his people’s good. Shared ground: both traditions draw from this line that God is not cruel, and both offer it gently to the afflicted as comfort rather than as an explanation of their pain.
